A neutral dark privacy film (the kind that looks mirrored or dark from outside during the day) will make it very hard to perceive curtain color at all from a passing car. This might be the least conspicuous option since it just looks like tinted glass.

- Test with a small piece first — hold the film against the curtain in daylight and view from outside
- Lighting matters: at night with interior lights on, colors read more true from outside. A darker film helps here
- Make sure whatever film you apply is removable (most are, but check) since you're renting

Navy blue is a dark, cool color. To make it appear neutral (like grey or black) from the outside, you need to introduce the **complementary color** into the light path.

Do not use permanent automotive tint, as it is difficult to remove and can cause thermal stress on residential glass (which may crack it). Instead, look for:

During the day, they reflect the sky/surroundings, making it impossible to see the color of the curtains inside. At night, however, if your lights are on, the effect reverses.

3.  If the navy is still too vibrant, add a **white or light grey sheer curtain** behind the navy ones. This will act as a neutral backdrop, making the navy look like a dark shadow rather than a distinct blue.

Dealing with a landlord who has a vendetta against a primary color is definitely a unique situation. 

While your idea of a color-shifting film is incredibly creative, **it won't work the way you want it to because of how light physics works.** Window films don't *change* the color of light; they *filter* (block) it. To stop blue light from reflecting outside, you would have to apply a yellow, orange, or red tinted film. This would make your windows look bright orange or yellow from the outside, which your landlord would likely also hate, and it would cast a weird colored glow into your room during the day.

Fortunately, because many strict HOAs and landlords require all windows to look uniform from the outside (usually white or beige), there are several renter-friendly workarounds that will let you keep your expensive navy curtains without him ever knowing.

Here are the best ways to hide the blue from the outside:

### 1. The Curtain Liner Hack (Best & Cheapest Option)
Since they are blackout curtains, light isn't passing *through* them; the landlord is just seeing the daylight reflecting off the back of the fabric. You can easily change the outward-facing color without changing the curtains.
*   **How to do it:** Buy a cheap set of white or beige blackout liners (or even just cheap white fabric). You can attach them directly to the back of your navy curtains using safety pins, fabric tape, or curtain clips. 
*   **Why it works:** From the inside, you see your beautiful navy curtains. From the outside, the landlord just sees a standard white window treatment. 

### 2. The Double-Rod / Tension Rod Trick
If you don't want to pin anything to your expensive curtains, you can add a physical barrier between the curtains and the glass.
*   **How to do it:** Buy a cheap spring-loaded tension rod (the kind used for shower curtains) and place it inside the window frame, right up against the glass. Hang a cheap white sheet, white sheer curtains, or a white roller shade on it. 
*   **Why it works:** The white layer faces the street, completely blocking the navy curtains from view. 

### 3. Frosted or Decorative Static Cling Film
If you are dead-set on treating the glass itself, skip color filters and go for privacy film. 
*   **How to do it:** Buy a roll of **static cling** frosted window film (do not buy adhesive film, as it will leave a nightmare residue that your landlord will charge you for). You just spray the window with soapy water, press the film on, and squeegee it flat. 
*   **Why it works:** Frosted film scatters light. If your navy curtains are pulled closed behind a frosted window, the window will just look like a flat, opaque white/gray square from the outside. The landlord won't be able to discern any color behind it.

### 4. One-Way Mirror Film (Use with Caution)
You can apply a reflective "mirror" static cling film to the windows. During the day, the landlord will just see a reflection of the street. 
*   *The Catch:* Mirror film only works when it is brighter outside than it is inside. At night, if you have lights on in the room, the mirror effect reverses, and people can see straight inside. However, since you have *blackout* curtains, as long as they are pulled tightly closed at night, no light will escape, and the window will just look black from the outside. 
*   *The Second Catch:* Landlords who are crazy enough to ban the color blue often have clauses banning "tin foil" or reflective window treatments, so check your lease before doing this.

**The Verdict:** Go with **Option 1 or 2**. It is the standard, foolproof way to beat strict window-facing decor rules without altering the glass or risking your security deposit.

Films that truly cut blue transmission tend to have an **amber/neutral-warm tint** and may make the outside view look slightly warmer (or slightly reduced in brightness). If the film is too dark (low Visible Light Transmission), your interior may also become dim/oddly contrasted.

### Practical tip
Buy a **small sample/test** (or a small-cut roll) and compare evening appearance from outside before committing.

## 3) Installing window film (typical DIY adhesive film)
This is a general method for common “pressure-sensitive”/adhesive window films. Always follow the specific product directions, because some films are heat-activated or have different liners/adhesives.

- Film + instructions
- Measuring tape + straightedge/utility knife
- Ammonia-free glass cleaner (often recommended)
- Lint-free cloths/paper towels
- Spray bottle (some installers use a water + a *tiny* bit of dish soap “application solution”)

- Painter’s tape (optional for masking edges)

1. **Measure carefully** (leave a little extra for trimming).
2. **Clean the glass extremely well** (no dust, grease, or lint). Any speck will show as a defect.

8. **Trim excess** with a fresh blade, using the window frame as a guide.
9. **Let it cure** (some films settle immediately; others need 24–72 hours depending on adhesive type and temperature).

Here is the hard truth: **You cannot use a window film to turn blue light into another color.**

If you put a colored film over a blue object, one of two things will happen:
1.  **If you use a Blue Film:** It will make the curtains look even more blue.
2.  **If you use a Yellow/Orange Film (Blue’s opposite):** The blue light will be absorbed, making the curtains appear **black or dark grey**.

There is no film that can "shift" blue wavelengths to green or red. However, you can achieve your goal using **light manipulation** rather than color shifting. Here are the three best ways to hide the blue from your landlord.

### Option 1: Reflective One-Way Mirror Film (The Best Solution)
This is the industry standard for hiding window decor. It works on the principle of light intensity.

*   **How it works:** During the day, the outside world is brighter than the inside of your apartment. A reflective silver film acts like a mirror on the outside. Your landlord will drive by and see a reflection of the sky, trees, or street, not your curtains.
*   **The Result:** The window looks silver or grey from the outside. The blue curtains are completely invisible because the light from them is drowned out by the reflection.
*   **The Caveat:** At night, if you have your interior lights on and it is dark outside, the effect reverses (the outside becomes a mirror looking in). However, since you have blackout curtains, you likely won't have light leaking out, so the mirror effect will hold or simply look dark.

### Option 2: White Frost Film (The "Privacy" Solution)
If you apply a white frosted privacy film, it diffuses the light passing through the glass.

*   **How it works:** It scatters the light rays.
*   **The Result:** Instead of seeing a distinct navy color, the landlord will see a blurry, vague white or grey shape. It will be obvious you have something on the window, but the specific color "blue" will be lost in the diffusion. It simply looks like a privacy shade.

### Option 3: The "Color Correction" Attempt (High Risk)
If you are dead set on trying to filter the color, you would need a yellow or amber film (often sold as "Blue Light Blocking" for windows or "Amber privacy film").

*   **The Physics:** Blue objects absorb Red and Green light. They reflect Blue. If you put a Yellow film (which blocks Blue) over the window, the blue light from the curtains hits the film and gets trapped/absorbed.
*   **The Result:** The curtains will look **pitch black** from the outside.
*   **The Risk:** While the curtains won't look blue, having windows that look like black holes might be equally suspicious or unsightly to a picky landlord.

### Application Advice (To avoid damaging the glass)
Since you are renting, you need to ensure the film is **removable**. Do not buy permanent adhesive films, as they can damage the glass or leave residue that the landlord will definitely notice when you move out.

1.  **Buy "Static Cling" or "Removable" Film:** These use water to stick to the glass and peel off cleanly without adhesive.
2.  **The "Soapy Water" Method:** Mix a few drops of dish soap with water in a spray bottle. Spray the glass thoroughly. Apply the film. The soapy water allows you to slide it into position and squeegee out the bubbles. This ensures it stays put but removes easily later.

### Summary Recommendation
Go with **Reflective Silver Film (Static Cling)**. It is the only solution that actively hides the color of the curtains rather than just changing it. It makes the window look like a professional tint job, which is aesthetically pleasing and unlikely to draw the ire of a landlord who is specifically looking for "blue."

* **How it works:** If you apply a very dark, neutral window tint (like 5% VLT, often called "limo tint"), you are cutting out 95% of the light passing through the glass. Whatever microscopic amount of blue light the curtain reflects will be trapped in the dark tint. To the outside world, the window will just look pitch black.
* **The Catch:** It makes the room very dark during the day and alters the appearance of the window from the outside (making it obviously tinted). 

### Option 3: One-Way Mirror Film (The Misdirection Approach)
Reflective window films rely on lighting ratios. If it is brighter outside than inside, the window acts as a mirror to the outside world.
* **How it works:** Instead of trying to hide the blue color, you prevent the landlord from seeing the curtain at all. He will just see the sky or the street reflected in your window.

1. **The nature of blackout curtains:** Navy *blackout* curtains have a layer of black acrylic/foam on the back of them. That black layer absorbs light. You may be overestimating how visible the color actually is from outside.

If your landlord is as obsessive as you say, he is much more likely to notice a yellow-tinted or heavily mirrored window than he is to notice the dark grey back of a blackout curtain. 

**The cheapest test:** Before buying film, wait until nightfall. Turn on the lights in your room exactly how you normally would, go outside, and look at the window. If you don't see blue, you don't need a film. If you *do* see a faint blue glow, your easiest, least destructive fix is to put a cheap, neutral-colored roller shade behind the navy curtains to block that specific glow from reaching the glass.
